props.title: The Banishment
props.initialSlug: Zvyagintsev's adaptation of William Saroyan's work

sections.content: The Banishment (2007) represents Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev's haunting sophomore feature, following his acclaimed debut The Return (2003). Drawing clear inspiration from Andrei Tarkovsky's meditative style and Ingmar Bergman's family dramas like Scenes from a Marriage (1973), Zvyagintsev crafts a devastating portrait of a family's disintegration. The film's stark imagery, including the memorable opening tracking shot through an industrial wasteland, establishes the emotional desolation that permeates this tale of betrayal and miscommunication.

sections.content: The film's methodical pacing and visual metaphors align with other masterworks of slow cinema like Béla Tarr's The Turin Horse (2011) and Nuri Bilge Ceylan's Once Upon a Time in Anatolia (2011). Zvyagintsev uses the rural setting as both refuge and prison, reminiscent of how Tarkovsky employed landscape in The Sacrifice (1986). Konstantin Lavronenko's restrained performance as Alex carries the weight of masculine pride and failure that would become hallmarks of Zvyagintsev's later work.

The film's exploration of faith, guilt, and redemption connects to a broader tradition of spiritual cinema, from Robert Bresson's Diary of a Country Priest (1951) to Carlos Reygadas' Silent Light (2007). The way Zvyagintsev frames domestic spaces - making them feel simultaneously claustrophobic and empty - creates an atmosphere of mounting dread that influenced later Russian art house films like Kantemir Balagov's Beanpole (2019). sections.content: Mikhail Krichman's cinematography in The Banishment employs a desaturated palette and precise framing that would become signatures of his continued collaboration with Zvyagintsev through Loveless (2017). The film's visual approach shares DNA with other contemporary masters of the "slow cinema" movement like Lav Diaz's Norte, the End of History (2013) and Apichatpong Weerasethakul's Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010), where extended takes and careful composition create a hypnotic effect.
